title: Lamps, Bread, and a Blasphemy Case
overview: This chapter moves from the daily care of the holy tent's lamps and bread to the trial and execution of a man who cursed God's name, along with laws about matching punishment to harm.

parts.label: Lamps kept burning (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: The people supplied the finest olive oil, and the high priest Aaron tended the lamps on the gold lampstand from evening till morning, just outside the curtain hiding the ark (the sacred chest holding the covenant law). The steady light is often read as a sign that God's presence among the people never went out.

parts.label: Bread on the gold table (vv. 5-9)
parts.note: Twelve large loaves, widely understood as one for each tribe of Israel, were set out before the LORD every Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, "on behalf of the Israelites" as a lasting covenant (a binding agreement). Incense placed beside them was offered as a token portion to the LORD, and the week-old bread went to the priests to eat in the holy area.

parts.label: A man curses God's name (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: During a fight, a man with an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father cursed "the Name," meaning God's own personal name, but the text does not say exactly what he said or why his family background is mentioned. Since there was no clear ruling yet, he was held in custody while Moses waited to learn the LORD's decision.

parts.label: The ruling on blasphemy (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: Those who heard him laid their hands on his head, likely a formal way of confirming what they had witnessed, and the whole community was to stone him outside the camp. The same penalty applied to foreigners living among them as to Israelites.

parts.label: Equal justice for harm (vv. 17-22)
parts.note: Murder carried the death penalty, killing someone's animal required replacing it, and injuries were matched in kind: "eye for eye, tooth for tooth." Many scholars see this as a limit on revenge so the penalty could not exceed the harm, and later Jewish law applied it as money compensation rather than physical injury.

parts.label: The sentence carried out (v. 23)
parts.note: The chapter ends by stating that the people took the man outside the camp and stoned him, as the LORD had commanded Moses. The text adds no further comment.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether laws like death for blasphemy and "eye for eye" carry any lasting moral authority or applied only to ancient Israel, especially since Jesus quoted "eye for eye" when telling his followers not to retaliate (Matthew 5).
think: When someone insults what a community holds most sacred, what kind of response seems fair to you, and why?
